content: Gamma globulins, also known as immunoglobulins (Ig's), are a class of proteins found in the blood. They are identified based on their position during serum protein electrophoresis. Among these, immunoglobulins are the most clinically significant. Gamma globulin injections are administered to temporarily enhance a patient’s immune response against specific diseases. These injections are commonly used in individuals who have been exposed to hepatitis A or measles. They are also utilized to facilitate compatibility between a kidney donor and recipient, even when there is a mismatch in blood type or tissue compatibility. Additionally, gamma globulin injections are given to patients with immune deficiencies, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia or hyper IgM syndrome, who are unable to produce sufficient gamma globulins on their own. In modern medical practice, the use of gamma globulin injections has become less frequent compared to the past. For example, gamma globulin injections that were once recommended for travelers have largely been replaced by the hepatitis A vaccine. However, gamma globulin infusions remain a valuable treatment for certain immunological disorders, such as idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). In ITP, antibodies attack platelets, leading to critically low platelet counts. Gamma globulin appears to work by causing the spleen to ignore antibody-tagged platelets, allowing these platelets to survive and function normally. Gamma globulin injections have also shown significant benefits in patients suffering from Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (CFS), also referred to as Chronic Fatigue and Immune Dysfunction Syndrome (CFIDS), Myalgic Encephalitis, Chronic Epstein-Barr Virus, or Chronic Mononucleosis. Another proposed mechanism by which gamma globulin administration may help in autoimmune diseases is by overwhelming the body’s degradation pathways for gamma globulins. This overload shortens the half-life of harmful gamma globulins in the bloodstream, thereby reducing their pathological effects. An excess of gamma globulins in the blood is referred to as hypergammaglobulinemia. Disorders involving gamma globulins are collectively termed gammopathies, such as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Gamma globulin therapy has also been approved for specific disease treatments. For instance, intravenous gamma globulin was FDA-approved in 2004 for use in kidney transplant patients. This therapy helps reduce antibodies in patients with kidney failure, enabling them to accept a kidney from a donor with a different blood type (ABO-incompatible) or an otherwise unacceptable tissue match. Dr. Stanley Jordan at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles was a pioneer in developing this treatment.
